en: Success! Homage to all the Buddhas, Dharmas, and Noble Saṅghas.
Mental states are preceded by the mind; the mind is supreme, and they are swifter than the mind.
If one speaks or acts with a corrupted mind, [suffering follows].
Then suffering follows him, just as the track follows the wheel of a cart that is being drawn.
Mental states are preceded by the mind, have the mind as their chief, and are swift as the mind.
For with a corrupted mind, one speaks or acts;
thereafter, suffering follows him like the wheel follows the hoof of the ox that draws the cart.
Mental states are preceded by mind, have mind as their chief, and are made of mind. If one speaks or acts with a pure mind,
happiness follows one even as a shadow that never departs.
Mental states are preceded by the mind, have the mind as their chief, and are swift as the mind.
With a serene mind one speaks or acts;
happiness follows that person, just as a shadow follows its follower.
One who performs evil deeds grieves here, grieves after death, and grieves in both places;
seeing the defilement of his own actions, he grieves and is tormented.
Here one grieves, after death one grieves; for the doer of evil deeds grieves in both places.
Indeed, he grieves and laments when he beholds his own defiled deed.
One rejoices here, one rejoices after passing away; having performed meritorious deeds, one rejoices in both places.
Having seen for oneself the purity of one’s own karma, one truly rejoices.
One rejoices here, one rejoices after passing away; indeed, the doer of merit rejoices in both places.
For he rejoices and exults upon seeing his own purified action.
"He reviled me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me"—
those who harbor such thoughts do not find peace from their enmity.
"He reviled me, he spoke against me, he defeated me, he caused me to lose"—
for those who harbor such enmity in their hearts, that hostility is never extinguished.
"He abused me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me"—
in those who do not harbor such thoughts, enmity subsides.
"He reviled me, he spoke against me, he defeated me, he caused me to lose"—
those who do not harbor such thoughts here, their enmity is pacified.
One who dwells contemplating beauty, with the sense faculties unrestrained,
immoderate in food, lazy, and lacking in energy.

Māra indeed overcomes him who constantly perceives beauty, who is unrestrained in his senses, who lacks moderation in food, and who is deficient in wakefulness— just as the wind overthrows a weak tree.
Passion indeed overcomes him who dwells contemplating the unattractive, even though he is well-restrained in his senses, just as the wind overthrows a weak tree.
But one who is not intoxicated by food and has aroused energy—
Māra truly cannot overcome him, just as the wind cannot move a rocky mountain.

Passion does not overcome one who constantly contemplates the foul, who is well-restrained in his senses, who knows the proper measure in eating, and who is devoted to wakefulness; it cannot shake him, just as the wind cannot move a firm mountain.
If one should find a prudent companion who is wise, a fellow traveler, steadfast in noble conduct,
one should travel with him, having overcome all [obstacles], joyful and mindful.

If he should indeed find a prudent companion in this world, one who always conducts himself virtuously, he should wander with him, having overcome all worldly fluxes, with a contented mind and a self established in mindfulness.
If one does not find a prudent companion who is wise, a fellow traveler firm in the holy life,
then like a king abandoning his conquered kingdom, one should wander alone like a lone elephant in the Matanga forest.
If one does not find a wise companion in this world who is always truly virtuous,
then one should wander alone like a king abandoning a vast kingdom, and one should commit no evil deeds.
It is better to wander alone; there is no companionship with a fool.
One should wander alone and commit no evil deeds, free from concern, like an elephant in a forest thicket.
The conduct of one alone is better than having foolish companions;
one should wander alone and commit no evils, like an elephant in the forest with little concern.
He who transgresses the Dhamma out of desire, hatred, fear, or delusion—
his fame wanes like the moon in the dark fortnight.
He who does not transgress the Dhamma out of desire, hatred, fear, or delusion—
his fame increases like the moon in the bright fortnight.
Heedfulness is the path to the deathless; heedlessness is the path of death.
Those who are heedful do not die; those who are heedless are as if already dead.
Heedfulness is indeed the state of immortality; heedlessness is the state of death.
Those who are heedful do not die; those who are heedless are dead already.
The wise have understood this distinction regarding heedfulness:
they delight in heedfulness, finding joy in the domain of the Noble Ones.
Having understood this distinction of heedfulness,
the wise and noble one should always take delight in heedfulness, which is his own proper domain.
Those wise ones who meditate, being constant and always firm in their exertion, attain Nibbāna, the unsurpassed security from bondage.
Those who are heedful, constant, and always firm in their exertion—
the wise ones— touch Nirvana, the unsurpassed security from bondage.
Foolish and witless people devote themselves to negligence,
but the wise man guards heedfulness as his most excellent treasure.
Foolish people of dull intellect follow after negligence,
but the wise man guards heedfulness as a merchant guards his greatest wealth.
Vigilant among the heedless, wide awake among those who sleep, the wise man goes on ahead, leaving them behind like a swift horse leaving a weak one.
Vigilant among the heedless, wide awake while others sleep,
he leaves behind the weak horse like Bhadrāśva and goes toward the wise Sumedhas.
When the wise man drives away negligence with heedfulness,
having ascended the palace of wisdom, free from sorrow amidst sorrowing folk,
the steadfast one looks down upon the fools as one standing on a mountain peak looks upon those on the ground.
When the wise man dispels heedlessness with heedfulness,
having ascended the palace of wisdom, he remains free from sorrow while gazing upon the grieving populace— just as a steadfast man standing on a mountain looks down upon those on the ground.
But he who, having been heedless in the past, later becomes heedful,
illuminates this world like the moon freed from clouds.
But he who, having previously been heedless here, later indeed does not become heedless—
he illumines this world like the moon released from the clouds.
But he who, having been heedless in the past, later becomes heedful— he, being mindful, overcomes this clinging to the world.
But he who, having previously been heedless here, later indeed does not become heedless— he, it is said, transcends this attachment in the world.
The bhikkhu who values heedfulness and perceives danger in negligence is incapable of falling away; he is indeed close to Nibbāna.
The monk who delights in heedfulness and perceives danger in heedlessness is incapable of falling away; he is indeed close to Nirvana.
The monk who values heedfulness and perceives danger in negligence goes forth like a fire, burning away fetters both subtle and gross.
The monk who delights in heedfulness sees danger in negligence.
Like a fire consuming both subtle and gross fetters, proceed;
take delight in heedfulness and guard your mind well.
Lift yourselves out of the difficult passage, like an elephant stuck in the mud;
take delight in heedfulness and guard your own minds.
Just as an elephant does not rescue itself from the mud, those who delight in negligence do not rescue themselves; but the wise, restrained by virtue, do so.
They indeed attain that state at the proper time where one who has reached it does not grieve;
rejoice in heedfulness, but do not delight in the pursuit of sensual pleasures.
Dwelling thus, ardent, with a peaceful mind and free from agitation,
devoted to the calming of the mind, one may make an end of suffering.
One should rise up, one should not be negligent; one should practice the Dhamma of good conduct.
One who practices the Dhamma sleeps happily in this world and in the world beyond.
One should rise up and not be negligent; one should practice the Dharma well.
For the practitioner of Dharma sleeps in happiness, both in this world and in the next.
For one who is industrious, mindful, pure in action, and moderate in eating;
for one who is self-controlled, lives according to the Dharma, and is heedful—his fame increases.
For one who is industrious, mindful, pure in heart, observant in conduct, self-restrained,
living according to the Dharma, and vigilant, fame increases.
Through exertion, heedfulness, self-restraint, and self-control,
a wise person should make an island which the flood cannot overwhelm.
Through exertion, heedfulness, self-restraint, and self-control,
the wise person makes an island which the flood does not overwhelm.
One who does not exert himself when it is time to exert, though young and strong, being indolent and lacking resolve,
being lazy and with a mind of slackened intention— such a sluggard does not travel the path of wisdom.
One who lacks vigor at the times for exertion, though eloquent in speech, is lazy and devoid of hope;
always defeated by his own conceptualizations and indolent, he never knows the path to wisdom.
One should not follow an inferior doctrine, nor dwell in negligence;
one should not follow wrong views, nor be a prosperer of the world.
One should not practice base dharmas, nor dwell in negligence;
one should not take pleasure in the view of nihilism, nor become one who increases the world.
One is not a bearer of the Dhamma merely by speaking much; rather,
he who, having heard even a little of the Dhamma, touches it with his body and does not neglect the Dhamma— he indeed is a bearer of the Dhamma.
One is not a bearer of the Dharma merely by speaking much; rather, he who,
having heard even a little of the Dharma here, truly realizes it with his body—
he indeed is a bearer of the Dharma, for he does not neglect the Dharma.
Investigate the Dhamma with heedfulness; let not the strands of sensual pleasure cause your mind to wander.
Let not the heedless man, having swallowed an iron ball, cry out in agony while being burned, "This is suffering!"
Dwell ardent and vigilant; let not the quality of sensual pleasure disturb your mind.
Do not, out of negligence, swallow a red-hot iron ball, lest you cry out while being cooked in the hells.
The Chapter on Heedfulness:
O Brahmin, cut the thread; exerting yourself, drive away existence, O Brahmin.
Having known the destruction of all conditioned formations, you are one who does not speak, O Brahmin.
Exerting yourself, cut off the stream; O Brahmin, cast away desires!
For once you have realized the exhaustion of all conditioned things, you will indeed be one who knows no [further] debt.
Whosoever one may know to possess the Dhamma, whether they be old or young,
one should pay them respectful homage, just as a Brahmin honors the sacred fire-sacrifice.
Whether it be an elder or a youth, one should pay homage to him from whom one may learn the Dharma,
just as a twice-born man honors the Agnihotra fire with devotion.
One should honor that very Dhamma taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One,
just as a brahmin honors the sacrificial fire.
One who understands the Dharma taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One should honor it with reverence and pay homage to it, just as a twice-born man honors the sacred fire-sacrifice.
One does not become a brahmin by matted hair, nor by lineage, nor by birth; rather, he who wards off evils, both small and great, in every way, is a brahmin.
One who indeed carries away evils is called a brahmin;
a brahmin is not defined by matted hair, nor by lineage, nor by birth. Rather, he who carries away evils—both subtle and gross—in every respect is known as a brahmin.
But because he has driven away all evils, he is indeed called a Brāhmaṇa.
Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, nor as dust to the point of an awl, so it is with those who possess taints.
He who is not defiled by sensual pleasures— him I call a brahmin;
like water on a lotus leaf, or a mustard seed on the point of an awl, he who is not smeared by desires— I indeed call him a brahmin.
The sun shines by day; the moon illuminates the night.
The armored warrior shines; the meditating brahmin shines.
Then, throughout all days and nights, the Buddha blazes with splendor.
By day the sun shines; by night the moon glows.
The armored Kṣatriya shines; the meditating Brāhmaṇa shines.
But the Buddha always, day and night, shines with splendor.
One for whom neither the near shore nor the far shore, nor both the near and far shores,
exist— one who is free from fever and disjoined [from bonds]— him I call a brahmin.
When a brahmin has reached the further shore regarding all phenomena, then all his fetters come to an end for him as he knows them.
For when a brahmin becomes one who has reached the further shore of his own duties, then all his attachments pass away as he perceives this.
He is indeed one whose fetters are destroyed, whose conceit and renewed existence are exhausted;
dwelling with the Saṅgha and established in the Dhamma, that possessor of knowledge does not enter into the Saṅgha.
But he, whose fetters are destroyed, whose pride is exhausted, and who is free from substrate,
having attained extinction, does not enter into reckoning as a conscious being after the breaking up of the body.
One should utter speech that is gentle, refined, and true;
with such speech one should not revile anyone—that person I call a brahmin.
He who always speaks words that are neither harsh nor deceptive, and by which no one is provoked to resentment— I indeed call him a brahmin.
Unassociated with both householders and homeless wanderers, not seeking a home, and possessing few desires— him I call a brahmin.
One who is unmixed with householders and likewise with those who have gone forth, who wanders without a home and is contented— I indeed call him a brahmin.
He who has committed no wrong by body, speech, or mind, being restrained in these three ways— him I call a brahmin.
He who has committed no evil deed through body, speech, or mind,
and who is well-restrained in these three ways— him indeed I call a brahmin.
Do not strike a brahmin, lest that brahmin should not release you;
woe to the slayer of a brahmin, who shall never be released from his debt.
One should not strike a brahmin, nor should a brahmin release [anger] against one; fie upon the slayer of a brahmin, and fie upon him who releases [anger]!
The Brahmin who slays his mother, slays a reciter, slays a king, and slays two Kshatriyas, as well as a kingdom with its followers, wanders free from affliction.
Having slain mother and father, a king, and two Vedic scholars,
and having destroyed a kingdom along with its subjects, a Brahmin goes forth free from sin.
One who possesses profound wisdom, who is intelligent, skilled in discerning the path from what is not the path, and who has attained the supreme goal— him I call a brahmin.
I call him indeed a brahmin who possesses profound intelligence, is rich in wisdom, is skilled in discerning the right and wrong paths, and has attained the supreme goal.
One who meditates, free from passion, seated, having done what was to be done, free from taints, and attained the supreme goal— him I call a brahmin.

I call him indeed a brahmin who meditates, who is free from passion, who has accomplished what was to be done, who is without intoxicants, whose taints are exhausted, and who is liberated from bondage.
The Chapter on Brahmins:
Restraint everywhere is good; restraint everywhere is truly good.
A monk who is restrained in all respects is liberated from all suffering.
Restraint of the body is good; restraint of speech is good;
restraint of the mind is also good; restraint in all things is good. A monk who is restrained in all things is liberated from all suffering.
Restraint of the body is good; restraint of speech is good;
restraint of the mind is good; restraint in all things is good. A monk who is restrained in all things is liberated from all suffering.
Restrained in hand, restrained in foot, restrained in speech, and with senses guarded.
Delighting in the internal, composed, alone, and contented—him they call a bhikkhu.
Restrained in hand, restrained in foot, restrained in speech, restrained in all ways; for he who delights in the internal, is composed, alone, and truly contented—he indeed is a bhikkhu.
With body stilled, mind stilled, and speech stilled, he is well-composed.
The monk who has vomited up the bait of the world is called "tranquil. With body stilled, mind stilled, and speech stilled, being well-composed,
the monk who has vomited up the bait of the world is declared to be "tranquil."
The monk who is restrained in speech, who speaks with wisdom, and who is not agitated;
He teaches the goal and the Dharma; his speech is sweet.
A monk who is restrained in speech, speaking softly and not being agitated, teaches the goal and the Dharma; his speech is sweet.
One should not despise one's own gain, nor should one live by envying the gains of others.

A monk who longs for the gains of others does not attain concentration; he should not despise his own acquisitions, nor should he be envious of others. A monk who envies others does not attain concentration.
Even if a monk receives little, he does not despise that gain.
The gods indeed praise that person who lives with purity and is free from sloth.
Even if one possesses little knowledge, if they are well-established in moral conduct,
the wise praise them as one who lives purely and is free from sloth.
Empty this boat, O monk; once emptied, it will become light for you. Having abandoned both passion and hatred, you will then reach Nibbāna.
Bail out this boat, O monk; once bailed out, it will become light. Having abandoned passion and hatred, you shall thereafter attain Nirvana.
With an uplifted mind and a joyful heart, having overcome both the pleasant and the unpleasant.
Then, full of gladness and mindful, let the bhikkhu wander forth, with a joyful heart and a serene mind, having overcome both the pleasant and the unpleasant.
A monk who abounds in joy shall attain the destruction of suffering;
a monk who dwells in loving-kindness and has faith in the Buddha's teaching [shall likewise do so].
He penetrated the peaceful state, the blissful stilling of all conditioned formations;
even in this very life, he realized Nibbāna, the unsurpassed security from bondage.
The monk who dwells in loving-kindness and has faith in the Buddha’s teaching shall attain the peaceful state, the blissful cessation of all conditioned formations.
(Nirvana, the supreme security from bondage, is realized in this very life.
For the monk who has entered an empty dwelling with a peaceful mind,
there is superhuman joy as he correctly perceives the Dhamma.
For the monk who has entered an empty dwelling, whose mind is set free,
and who perceives the Dharma correctly, there arises a non-human delight.
To whatever extent one correctly contemplates the arising and passing away of the aggregates, one gains gladness of mind; for this is the cause of the deathless for one who understands.
In whatever way he contemplates the arising and passing away of the aggregates,
he gains therein great joy and abundant happiness;
then, filled with such joy and mindful, the bhikṣu should wander forth.
There is no meditative absorption for one lacking wisdom, and there is no wisdom for one who does not practice meditation;
he in whom both absorption and wisdom exist is indeed close to Nibbāna.
For one lacking wisdom there is no meditation, and for one who meditates without wisdom there is no wisdom;
he who possesses both meditation and wisdom is indeed near to Nirvana.
In this regard, this is the beginning for a wise bhikkhu:
restraint of the sense faculties, contentment, and discipline according to the Prātimokṣa.
This is the beginning for that wise monk:
contentment, guarding of the sense faculties, and restraint according to the Prātimokṣa.
One should associate with friends who are auspicious, living pure and untiring; one should be skillful in conduct and maintain the continuity of the lineage.
Then, full of gladness and mindful, a bhikkhu should wander forth.

One should associate with those who are worthy, always maintain a pure livelihood, live by means of receiving alms, and be skilled in proper conduct; then, full of joy and mindful, a bhikṣu should wander forth.
When needs arise, a friend is a joy; merit is a joy at the end of life.
Contentment is a joy for one who has nothing; the abandonment of all evil is a joy.
When wealth has arisen, companions are happiness; merit is happiness at the time of the end of life;
contentment with whatever one has is happiness; and the cessation of all suffering is happiness.
Motherhood is happiness in the world, and fatherhood is happier than that; the state of a recluse is happiness in the world, and the state of a brahmin is happier than that.
Happy is the state of being a maternal uncle in this world, and happy indeed is the state of being a paternal uncle;
happy is the state of being a śramaṇa in this world, and likewise happy is the state of being a brāhmaṇa.
Virtue is happiness as long as one reaches old age; well-established faith is happiness;
speech that has the essence of truth is happiness; and the destruction of conceit is happiness.
Virtue is happiness until old age; happiness is faith firmly established;
happiness is speech devoted to the goal; and the non-doing of evil is happiness.
The arising of Buddhas is blissful; the teaching of the Dharma is blissful;
the harmony of the Saṅgha is blissful; and the ascetic practice of those who are harmonious is blissful.
Happy is the arising of a Buddha; happy is the teaching of the Dharma;
happy is the harmony of the Saṅgha; and happy is the ascetic practice of those who are united.
Happy is the sight of the noble ones, and dwelling together with the virtuous is also happy;
by not seeing fools, one would always be happy.
Seeing the noble ones is happiness, and dwelling together with them is always happiness;
by not seeing fools, one shall be happy forever.
For one who associates with fools indeed grieves for a long time;
dwelling with fools is always painful, like being with enemies. But the wise are pleasant to dwell with, like a reunion with kinsmen.
For one who associates with fools wanders for a long journey in sorrow;
indeed, dwelling with fools is painful in every respect, like living with enemies. But dwelling with the wise is pleasant, like a reunion with kinsmen.

For one should serve such a wise and highly learned man, who possesses the noble conduct and vows of steadfastness and is a noble being of great intelligence, just as the moon follows the path of the stars.
One should attend upon one who is steadfast, wise, virtuous, and learned—
one who is a leader endowed with speed, just as the hosts of stars attend upon the moon.
From what is dear arises suffering; from what is dear comes grief, from what is dear comes fear.
For one who is completely liberated from what is dear, there is no grief—how could there be fear?
From the beloved arises sorrow; from the beloved arises fear.
For those who are completely liberated from the beloved, there is no sorrow—how then could there be fear?
Do not associate with those who are dear, nor ever with those who are unpleasant;
for not seeing the dear is suffering, as is seeing the unpleasant.
May there never be union with those who are dear, nor may there ever be [union] with those who are unpleasant;
for not seeing those who are dear is suffering, as is seeing those who are unpleasant.
One should not form affection for that [world], for attachment to what is dear leads to evil;
indeed, those for whom there is neither the dear nor the undear find no knots within.
Therefore, one should not act for the sake of what is dear, for the state of being dear is evil. Those for whom there is neither the dear nor the undear have no knots.
Hunger is the foremost of diseases; conditioned phenomena are the foremost of sufferings.
Having known this as it truly is, one realizes that Nibbāna is the supreme happiness.
Hunger is the supreme of diseases, and conditioned formations are indeed suffering;
knowing this as it truly is, one should be intent upon Nirvana.
Health is the supreme gain; contentment is the supreme wealth; trust is the supreme kinsman; Nibbāna is the supreme happiness.
Health is the supreme gain; contentment is the supreme wealth;
trust is the supreme friend; and Nirvana is the supreme happiness.
If one sees extensive happiness in the relinquishing of limited happiness,
the wise person should abandon the limited happiness, clearly perceiving the extensive happiness.
He who, by relinquishing limited pleasure, perceives a vast happiness—
that wise person, seeing that vast happiness, should abandon limited pleasure.
For a person who is always mindful, knowing the proper measure in food obtained through alms, his afflictions become thin; he ages slowly, preserving his life.
For a person who is always mindful and knows the proper measure of food, his afflictions become slight; he ages slowly while preserving his life-force.
A person of noble birth is rare; he is not born everywhere.
Wherever that hero is born, that family prospers in happiness.
A person of noble birth is difficult to find; he is not born everywhere.
Wherever that hero is born, that family prospers in happiness.
In all circumstances, indeed, the virtuous are steadfast; being free from desire for sensual pleasures, the good do not prattle on.
When questioned by happiness or by suffering, the virtuous do not act with fluctuation.
Virtuous people possess a sense of shame; the noble do not prattle for the sake of desire.
For when touched by suffering or by happiness, virtuous people do not become fickle.
Victory gives rise to enmity; the defeated one lies in misery.
Having abandoned both victory and defeat, the one who is tranquil sleeps in happiness.
Victory engenders enmity; the defeated one sleeps in misery.
Having abandoned both victory and defeat, the one who is tranquil sleeps happily.
Happy are the rivers with their pleasant landing-stairs; happy is the person who has conquered through the Dharma;
happy is the acquisition of faith; and the non-doing of evil is happiness.
Happy is the river with its excellent landing-stairs; happy is the Conqueror who has triumphed through the Dharma;
the constant attainment of wisdom is happiness; and the non-doing of evil is happiness.
It is a joy to behold those who possess virtuous conduct; it is a joy to behold those who are deeply learned;
it is also a joy to behold the Arhats, who are fully liberated and free from all substrata of existence.
It is a joy to behold those who possess virtuous conduct; it is a joy to behold those who are deeply learned;
and it is a joy to behold Arhats who are completely liberated from rebirth.
Whatever sorrows or lamentations, or whatever various forms of suffering exist in the world, all these arise in dependence upon the beloved; when the beloved is absent, these do not come to be.
For indeed, grief, lamentation, and the manifold sufferings of the world all arise in dependence upon what is dear; if that which is dear did not exist, none of this would ever come to be.
For those who have nothing dear to them in this world are happy and free from sorrow;
therefore, desiring that sorrowless and stainless state, one should not hold anything dear anywhere in the world.

Therefore, those for whom there is nothing whatsoever dear are indeed happy and free from sorrow. Thus, seeking the state that is beyond grief, one should not form attachments in the world of the living.
For one who has traversed the path, who is free from sorrow, who is liberated in every respect,
and for whom all feverish cravings have been abandoned, no burning anguish exists.
For one who has traversed the path, who is free from sorrow, who is fully liberated, a protector,
and who has abandoned all fetters, no fever exists.
For those who have no accumulation and who have fully understood food,
their track is difficult to follow, like that of birds in the sky.
For those who have no accumulation and who have fully understood food,
their track is as difficult to follow as that of birds in the sky.
The mind of one who is liberated through right knowledge, who is tranquil, and who is a protector, becomes peaceful; his speech and his actions are also peaceful.
The mind of this monk becomes tranquil, and his speech and bodily actions are tranquil,
for he is a bhikṣu who is perfectly liberated through right knowledge and is thoroughly stilled.
For one whose faculties have attained composure, like well-tamed horses by a charioteer,
for that protector who has abandoned conceit and is free from taints, even the gods yearn.
For one whose senses have attained equanimity, like a well-trained horse under a charioteer,
even the gods always envy him who has abandoned all faults and is free from outflows.
They lead the tamed one to the assembly; the king mounts the tamed one.
Among men, the tamed one is supreme—he who endures abusive speech.
The self-controlled indeed goes to the assembly; the self-controlled king mounts [his throne];
the self-controlled man who endures harsh speech is the best among men.
Better than well-trained mules, or noble Sindh horses,
or great tusker elephants, is one who has tamed himself.
For one who might tame a noble horse, a well-bred steed from Sindh,
or a great elephant of the Kuñjara breed— the self, when tamed, is better than that.
For one does not reach that state by means of those who know or do not know,
as one who is tamed goes by means of oneself well-tamed.
For one who is self-subdued does not reach that state by means of that vehicle,
which the subdued man reaches by means of his own well-tamed self.
Just as a solid mass of rock is not moved by the wind,
so too the wise are not moved by blame or praise.
Just as a solid mass of rock is not shaken by the wind,
so too the wise are not moved by blame or praise.
He who wears the saffron robe while being free from impurity,
yet devoid of self-control and truthfulness, is not worthy of the saffron robe.
He who, being free from passion, shall wear the saffron robe—
yet lacking self-control and virtuous conduct— is not worthy of that saffron robe.
But he who has vomited out impurities, who is well-composed in his virtues,
and who is endowed with self-control and truth— he indeed is worthy of the saffron robe.
But he who has vomited out impurities, who is well-composed in his moral virtues, and who is endowed with self-control and gentleness— he indeed deserves the saffron robe.
The Chapter on Sorrow:
O virtuous one, advance toward what is wholesome; restrain the mind from evil.
For one who performs merit with delay, the mind delights in evil.
One should hasten toward what is wholesome and restrain the mind from evil; for the mind of one who performs merit sluggishly delights in sinful things.
If a person should commit an evil deed, he should not do it again and again;
one should not take pleasure in it, for the accumulation of evil is suffering.
If a person commits evil through action, he would not do it again and again;
one should not take pleasure in that, for the accumulation of evil is suffering.
If a person should perform merit, and should perform it again and again, one should direct one's desire toward that very thing; for the accumulation of merit is blissful.
A person should perform meritorious deeds and should perform them again and again;
one should take delight therein, for the accumulation of merit brings happiness.
For one who is always pure, there is always the Phaggū festival; for one who is pure, there is always the Uposatha.
For one who is pure and whose deeds are clean, the vow is always fulfilled.

For one who is always pure, the observance is always fruitful; for one who is always pure, the poṣadha is always fulfilled; for one who is pure and whose actions are clean, the vow is always successfully accomplished.
An ill deed not done is better; an ill deed torments later.
One grieves thinking, "An ill deed was done by me," and grieves even more when gone to a state of woe.
It is better not to do an evil deed than to do it; for an evil deed burns later.
One grieves after having committed an evil deed, and one grieves when gone to a miserable rebirth.
A deed well done is good, for the doer does not regret it;
thinking "I have done this well," he rejoices, and having gone to a happy destination, he rejoices even more.
A well-performed deed is truly beneficial, for having performed it, one does not regret it;
having performed a good deed, one rejoices, and having gone to the next world, one rejoices there as well.
Even a wicked person sees what is auspicious as long as his evil does not ripen;
but when the evil ripens, then the wicked person sees his own evils.
Even a wicked person sees what is auspicious as long as his evil does not ripen;
but when the evil ripens, then he perceives evils.
Even a good person sees evil as long as the good has not ripened;
but when the good ripens, then the good person sees what is good.
Even a virtuous person sees evil as long as his virtue has not yet ripened; but when his virtue ripens, then he beholds auspicious things.
Even for one who commits evil, there is prosperity as long as the evil does not ripen;
but when the time arrives, the evildoer sees the consequences of his evil deeds.
Even for one performing a good deed, evil does not ripen as long as the good has not yet matured;
but when the time arrives, the doer of good beholds the fruits of their goodness.
If there were no wound on one's hand, one would not take poison with the hand;
poison does not enter that which is unwounded, and for one who does nothing evil, there is no suffering.
There would be no wound on his hand, yet he could hold poison in his hand;
for poison does not penetrate where there is no wound, and there is no sin for one who does nothing wrong.
For an evil deed that has been committed does not remain stagnant like thickened milk;
burning, it follows the fool, like a fire covered by ashes.
For an evil deed committed does not curdle immediately like milk;
burning the fool, it follows him like a fire covered by ashes.
For an evil deed committed does not cut like a sword;
rather, having passed away, one knows the destination of the evildoer.
For an evil deed does not cut like a sword immediately;
rather, one knows in the next world what destination belongs to those who have committed evil deeds.
One should perform what is to be done before it has come; let not what is to be done afflict you at the time when it must be done.
For one who performs such duties beforehand, no duty shall afflict them at the time when it must be done.

For one should attend to what is to be done beforehand, so that my duty may not fail when the time for action arrives. For one who acts with constant readiness, his duty never fails at the time for action.
One should do beforehand that which one knows to be for one's own welfare;
a wise person does not follow the counsel of a mere cart-driver when it comes to exertion.
One should do immediately that which one knows to be for one's own welfare;
a wise person should not proceed sluggishly with the deliberations of a cartwright.
Just as a cartwright, having left the level highway for a great road,
encounters a rugged path and sits there brooding with his axle broken.
Just as a cartwright, having abandoned a level highway for a great road and then encountered a rugged path, grieves bitterly when his axle breaks.
Thus, having turned away from the Dharma and followed what is contrary to the Dharma,
the fool, fallen into the jaws of death, lies brooding like one whose eyes have been plucked out.
Thus, having departed from dharma and followed adharma,
the fool falls under the power of death and grieves like one whose eyes have been plucked out.
Many with saffron robes around their necks, of evil character and unrestrained,
being wicked through their wicked deeds, have been reborn in hell.
Many with saffron robes around their necks are indeed of evil nature and unrestrained;
for by their evil deeds, these evildoers go from here to a miserable rebirth.
The speaker of untruth goes to hell, as does he who, having done a deed, says, "I did not do it.
Both these men, having passed away, become equal in the next world—those who have performed base actions.
The speaker of untruth goes to the hells, as does he who performs other such actions here; for both those men, having practiced base conduct, are declared to be equal after death in the next world.
The evil that a man who is not corrupted brings upon another person who is pure, virtuous,
and blameless, falls back upon that fool himself, like fine dust thrown against the wind.
For the evil that is cast against a man who is uncorrupted, pure, and eternally free from stain,
recoils upon that very fool, just like dust thrown against the wind.
Like a merchant on a perilous road with little escort but great wealth,
or like one desiring life avoiding poison, one should avoid evil deeds.
Just as a merchant on a perilous road with little wealth but great riches,
or one who desires life while facing poison, should avoid evils.
He who desires his own happiness by inflicting suffering upon others is entangled in the contact of enmity and is not released from suffering.
He who desires his own happiness by inflicting suffering upon others is entangled in the bonds of enmity and is not liberated from suffering.
The stench of a corpse fades away after three nights, even if it has been left out;
but for a man who walks in unrighteousness, the foul odor does not fade at all.
Just as householders who possess abundant jewels, when their city is set ablaze and burning,
exert themselves for the sake of pearls, gems, crystals, and silver, thinking, "Perhaps we might carry something out."

In just this way, ascetics of abundant wisdom, noble ones training in the noble paths, terrified by the fear of birth, old age, and death, and afflicted by suffering, exert themselves, thinking: "May we attain peace."
In the Chapter on the Worthy,
it is said: "The fragrance of flowers does not go against the wind, nor does that of sandalwood, tagara, or vāhlika."
But the fragrance of the virtuous goes against the wind; the person of noble character wafts in all directions.
The fragrance of flowers does not go against the wind, nor that produced from tagara or sandalwood;
but the fragrance of the virtuous goes against the wind—the person of noble character wafts in all directions.
Whether it be sandalwood, tagara, blue lotus, or vāsikī—
among all these varieties of fragrance, the fragrance of virtue is unsurpassed.
Compared to tagara, sandalwood, vārṣika, and likewise the blue lotus—
from among all these types of fragrances, the fragrance of ethical discipline is unsurpassed.
This fragrance of tagara and sandalwood is but slight;
however, the fragrance of those possessed of virtue wafts even among the gods, being supreme.
For this scent of tagara and sandalwood is indeed slight;
but the fragrance of those who possess virtuous conduct wafts even among the gods.
For those who are perfected in virtue, who dwell in heedfulness,
and who are liberated through right knowledge, Māra does not find their path.
For those of pure conduct who dwell in heedfulness and are liberated through right knowledge, Māra does not find their path.
Just as a beautiful flower may be colorful yet lacking fragrance,
so too well-spoken words are fruitless for one who does not act upon them.
Just as a beautiful flower may possess color but lack fragrance,
so too are well-spoken words fruitless for one who does not act upon them.
Just as a beautiful flower that is both colorful and fragrant,
so too the well-spoken word becomes fruitful for one who acts upon it.
Just as a beautiful flower may be both colorful and fragrant,
so too does well-spoken speech bear fruit for one who acts upon it.
Just as a bee, without harming the color or fragrance of a flower,
flies away taking its nectar, so should a sage conduct himself in a village.
Just as a bee departs from a flower, taking its nectar without harming its color or fragrance, so should a sage conduct himself among a village.
While a man is gathering flowers, his mind distracted, death seizes him and departs, just as a great flood sweeps away a sleeping village.
Death carries away a man who is gathering flowers with a distracted mind, just as a great flood sweeps away a sleeping village.
While a man is gathering flowers with his mind distracted,
Death brings him under its power before his desires are fulfilled.
While a man is gathering flowers alone, his mind distracted and still unsated by sensual desires, the Ender brings him under his power.
Just as one might fashion many garlands from a heap of flowers,
so too should a mortal who has been born perform much that is wholesome;
just as one would make many garlands from heaps of flowers.
Thus, by a mortal who has been born, much wholesome merit should be performed.
Who shall conquer this earth, or this world of Yama together with its gods?
Who, being skilled, shall pick out [the essence] from the well-taught verses of Dharma, as one picks a flower?
Who shall conquer this earth, as well as the world of Yama together with its gods?
Who, being skillful, shall select the well-taught verses of Dharma like a flower?
The wise one will conquer the earth, and even this world of Yama together with its gods;
being skilled, he will cast off [defilements] like a flower, having well-expounded the verses on Dharma.
The learner shall conquer the earth, as well as the world of Yama together with its gods;
for he, being skilled, will gather the well-taught words of Dharma like a flower.
Just as the vāsśikī creeper sheds its flowers,
so too, O bhikkhus, cast off both lust and hatred.
Just as the vassika flower sheds its pollen during the rains, so too, O monks, cast off passion and hatred.
Having understood this world to be like foam and having fully awakened to its nature as a mirage,
one who cuts off Māra’s blossoming flowers shall go beyond the sight of the King of Death.
Having understood this body to be like foam and having fully awakened to its nature as a mirage,
one should cut off the flowers of Māra here and go beyond the sight of the King of Death.
Just as a lotus might spring up, pure-scented and delightful, upon a heap of refuse discarded by the great highway.
Just as a lotus might grow upon a heap of refuse discarded by the side of a great road— a lotus that is pure-scented and delightful— so too is this.
Thus, amidst the common people who have become like a heap of refuse and are like the blind,
the disciples of the Perfectly Enlightened One shine forth with their wisdom.
Thus, in this world which has become like a heap of refuse and where ordinary people are like the blind,
the disciples of the Perfectly Enlightened One shine forth with wisdom.
The Chapter on Flowers:
Craving increases like a creeping vine for the person who wanders heedlessly.
Seeking fruit, she leaps from tree to tree in the forest like a monkey.
For a person who acts with negligence, craving increases like the wind;
he wanders again and again through saṃsāra, like a monkey in the forest seeking fruit.
But for one who endures this craving, which is difficult to overcome in the world,
sorrows increase like weeds growing in a marsh.
He who tolerates this worldly craving, so difficult to abandon,
finds his sorrows increase like *bīraṇa* grass when drenched with rain.
But whoever endures this vile craving, so difficult to overcome in the world—
for him sorrows roll away like drops of water from a lotus leaf.
But he who abandons this worldly craving, so difficult to cast off,
his sorrows cease like a drop of water from a lotus leaf.
I say this to you for your welfare, all you who have gathered here: dig up craving by its very roots, as one seeking usira root digs up the beruṇī.
When craving has been dug up by the roots, there is no sorrow; whence could fear arise?
Therefore, I speak this for your welfare, all you who have gathered here: dig up craving by its very roots, just as one seeking *uśīra* root digs up the *bīraṇa* grass.
For one who has dug out the root of craving, there is no sorrow; whence could there be fear?
Driven by craving, a person wanders through the long course of existence,
from this state to another state, here and there again and again.
Accompanied by craving, a person travels along the long road through hope;
thus, through the transformation of states of being, one undergoes coming and going within saṃsāra.
Having understood this danger— that craving is the origin of suffering—
the mindful monk, free from craving and without grasping, should wander forth.
Having understood this danger— that craving is the source of suffering—
a monk should wander forth mindful, free from craving and without grasping.
The wise say that the bond made of iron, wood, or hemp is not a firm one; rather, it is the longing for necklaces and earrings, and the dependence on sons and wives, that is the true fetter.
The Noble Ones do not call that a firm bond which is made of iron, wood, or *balbaja* grass;
rather, it is the attachment toward sons and wives that belongs to one of dull intellect whose mind is impassioned.
The wise call this a firm bond—carrying one away, subtle, and difficult to release.
Having severed even this, the virtuous go forth, free from longing, having abandoned all suffering.
The Noble Ones call this a firm bond, stable on all sides and difficult to release;
yet, having severed even this, they go forth as wanderers, indifferent, having abandoned the pleasure of sensual desires.

Not even by a rain of kārṣāpaṇas is there satisfaction found among sensual pleasures; for no gratification is found through desires, even those of the divine realm. He finds no delight even in celestial pleasures.
The disciple of the Fully Enlightened One delights in the destruction of craving.
Even toward divine sensual pleasures, he finds no delight.
The disciple of the Buddhas always delights in the exhaustion of craving.
Free from craving, without grasping, skilled in the expression of the unsurpassed,
he understands through the combination of syllables what precedes and what follows;
he, indeed, possessing his final body, is called one of great wisdom.
The joys of a living being are full of attachment and longing;
those who are addicted to pleasure and seek after happiness are indeed subject to birth and old age.
Indeed, beings possess flowing attachments and endearments that lead to mental pleasure;
those men who are bound by gratification and seekers of happiness truly approach birth and old age.
Led by craving, beings crawl about like a hare pursued by a predator;
attached by the bonds of perception and attachment, they enter the womb again and again for a long time.
Enveloped by cravings, living beings run about like hares in a snare;
clinging through fetters, they undergo suffering again and again for a long time.
Release in the past, release in the future, release in the middle; having gone beyond existence with a mind liberated in every respect, you shall not again undergo birth and old age.

Release what is before, release what is behind, and release what is in the middle; having reached the further shore of existence, with a mind liberated in every respect, you shall not again undergo birth and old age.
Behold this person: though freed from the forest by reaching the state beyond the forest, being freed from the forest, he runs back toward the forest itself;
released, he runs right back to his bonds.
Behold this person who, though liberated by those seeking nirvāṇa and freed from the forest, runs right back into the forest; though released, he runs toward bondage itself.
Fields have weeds as their defect; this generation has passion as its defect.
Therefore, what is given to those free from passion bears great fruit.
Fields have weeds as their defect; this generation has passion as its defect. Therefore, what is given to those free from passion yields great fruit.
Fields have weeds as their defects; this progeny has faults as its defects.
For what is given to those who are free from defects bears great fruit.
Fields have weeds as their defect; this generation has hatred as its defect.
Therefore, what is given to those free from hatred becomes of great fruit.
Fields have weeds as their defect; this generation has delusion as its defect.
Therefore, what is given to those who are free from delusion yields great fruit.
Fields have weeds as their defect; this generation has delusion as its defect.
Therefore, what is given to those free from delusion yields great fruit.
Truly delightful is the forest where people do not find pleasure; those free from passion will delight there, but others who seek after sensual desires will not.
The forests are delightful, yet people do not find pleasure therein;
those free from passion will rejoice here, but not those who seek after sensual desires.
Just as a tree, even when cut down, grows forth again if its root is firm and undamaged, even so,
if the underlying tendency of craving is not uprooted, this suffering arises again and again.
Just as a tree, even when cut down, grows forth once again if its roots are never harmed,
so too, as long as the latent tendencies of craving have not been uprooted, this suffering arises again and again.
The Veda has non-recitation as its impurity; the household has lack of exertion as its impurity.
Laziness is the stain of beauty; negligence is the stain of those who guard [their senses].
Evil conduct is a stain; stinginess is a stain for those who give;
evil deeds are a stain in this world and in the world beyond.
Beyond that, I declare ignorance to be the stain; death is the stain.
For those who have abandoned these stains, the bhikkhus are stainless.
Just as rust arising from iron, once produced, consumes that very iron,
even so do one's own deeds lead the one who lives in negligence to a state of misery.
For rust arises from iron, and once arisen, it consumes that very iron;
in the same way, one's own actions lead one who acts without reflection to a state of misery.
Your leaves have now turned pale, and the messengers of Yama stand before you;
you stand at the gateway of departure, and even provisions for the journey are not found for you.
Like a smith who, with effort and exertion, purifies silver by blowing upon it himself.
With stains cleansed and free from blemish, you have reached the second stage of the noble ones.
Gradually, little by little, moment by moment, the wise person should blow away their own impurities, just as a smith does with silver.
Gradually, little by little, moment by moment, the wise person should blow away his own impurities, just as a smith removes the dross from silver.
It is easy for one who is shameless, defiled, treacherous, insolent, as brave as a crow, and a thief, to live. But he lives a life of corruption.
It would be easy to live as one who is shameless, as bold as a crow, as ravening as a scavenger, and as impudent as a leaper; yet, such a life is lived here in a state of affliction.
But for one who possesses a sense of shame, who always seeks purity, who is unattached and free from arrogance, and who perceives a pure livelihood— it is difficult to live.
But for one who possesses a sense of shame, who is ever seeking purity, who is well-restrained, modest, pure in livelihood, and discerning, life here is indeed difficult to lead.
One clearly perceives the faults of others, yet finds one's own even more difficult to see;
here in this world, one winnows out the faults of others like chaff, while one’s own, however, the deceitful person hides like a gambler concealing his losing throw.
The faults of others are easy to see, but one's own faults are difficult to perceive;
another winnows away the faults of another like chaff,
while this deceitful person conceals his own, just as a rogue hides a dice-counter.
Evil deeds and those things which are harmful to oneself are easy to do;
but that which is beneficial and virtuous is indeed most difficult to perform.
For things that are unwholesome and detrimental to oneself are indeed easy to do;
but that which is truly beneficial and wholesome is indeed extremely difficult to accomplish.
Easy to do are things that are unwholesome and detrimental to oneself;
but those things that are wholesome and beneficial, the wise alone perform them.
They feel shame for what is not shameful, and they feel no shame for what is shameful;
perceiving fear where there is no fear, and perceiving no fear where there is fear,
beings who have embraced wrong views go to a state of misery.
Those who feel shame for what is not shameful, yet feel no shame for what is shameful;
those who see fear where there is no fear, and see no fear where there is fear—
through the adoption of wrong views, such beings go to an evil destiny.
Those who perceive what is blameless as blameworthy, and perceive what is blameworthy as blameless,
go to an evil destination because of their adherence to wrong view.
Those who perceive the essential in the unessential and the unessential in the essential do not attain the essential, for they range within the domain of wrong intention.
Those who perceive the essential in the unessential, and perceive the unessential in the essential,
do not attain the essential, for they dwell within the sphere of false conceptualization.
Having known the essential as essential and the non-essential as non-essential,
they attain the essential, for their range of activity is governed by right intention.
Having understood the essential as essential and the non-essential as non-essential,
those whose range of activity is right intention attain the essential.
One should apply oneself to what is meaningful and not apply oneself to what is meaningless;
having abandoned profit, one who grasps at what is pleasant envies those devoted to the pursuit of the goal.
Always engaging himself in what is improper and disengaging from what is proper,
he abandons the true meaning to seize upon what is merely pleasant, and thus he envies one who is devoted to the pursuit of the goal.
The Chapter on Defilements:
Fools of dull wit conduct themselves as if with an enemy, even with their own selves.
Performing an evil deed that results in bitter fruit.
For fools of poor wisdom act like enemies toward themselves,
performing evil deeds that result in bitter fruit.
And how is that deed performed which the doer regrets,
the ripening of which he experiences while weeping with a tearful face?
That action is not well done which, having been performed, one later regrets;
for one must experience its ripening while weeping with a tearful face.
And that deed is well done which, when performed, the doer does not regret,
and of which he, confident and joyful, experiences the result.
But that action is well-done which, having been performed, one does not regret;
being confident and glad of heart, one experiences its ripening.
To whatever extent knowledge arises for a fool only for his own harm,
it destroys the fool’s bright limb and causes his head to fall.
For as long as a fool is known only for his own harm,
he destroys the virtuous portion of the fool and shall cause his head to fall.
They desire the cultivation of non-existent qualities and precedence among the monks,
as well as lordship over monasteries and honor in other families.
The unvirtuous desire gain and honor among the monks,
as well as possessiveness regarding their dwellings and veneration from the families of others.
"Let both householders and those who have gone forth think that this was done by me alone;
they would not be capable of [discerning] anything whatsoever regarding what ought and ought not to be done."
May both householders and renunciants always know me alone;
may they be subject to my will in all matters, whether they ought to be done or not.
Such is the intention of the fool, and his desire and conceit increase;
for the basis for gain is one thing, while that which leads to Nibbāna is another.
Thus are the intentions of the fool, which increase desire and pride;
for the secret means to worldly gain is one thing, while that which leads to Nirvana is another.
Seeing this thus as it really is, a disciple of the Buddha should not delight in honor, but should cultivate seclusion.
Having understood this as it truly is, a disciple of the Buddhas should never delight in honor, but should instead cultivate solitude.
The fool indeed considers himself victorious when he speaks harsh words;
for the wise person who understands, victory consists in forbearance.
Indeed, the fool considers himself victorious by speaking harsh words;
but for him who endures the insults of others, victory is as constant as it is for the righteous.
The strength of one whose strength is the strength of a fool is actually no strength at all; for one who possesses strength and is guarded by the Dhamma, there exists no adversary.
For the strength of one whose strength lies in anger is indeed no strength;
for one who is angry and devoid of dharma, there is no right practice.
The fool who considers himself a fool is actually wise in that regard;
but the fool who considers himself wise is indeed called a fool.
The fool who knows "I am a fool" is a wise man;
but the fool who fancies himself wise is called a fool indeed.
Long is the night for one who sleeps, long is the league for one who is weary;
long is saṃsāra for fools who do not understand the true Dhamma.
Long is the night for one who stays awake; long is the league for one who is weary;
long is saṃsāra for the fool who does not understand the true Dharma.
The man who touches a putrid fish even with the tip of a blade of kusha grass—the kusha grass itself becomes foul; such is the consequence of associating with fools.
Just as a man who ties a rotten fish to the tip of a blade of kusha grass finds even that kusha grass becoming foul with its odor, so too does one who cultivates evil become tainted by it.
Just as a man who wraps tagara in a palāśa leaf causes even that leaf to smell fragrant, so too is the influence of attending upon the wise.
Just as a man who wraps tagara with a leaf of the palāśa tree makes even those leaves fragrant through constant association with the virtuous, so it is with the company of the good.
Even if one does not commit evil oneself, if one associates with those who do,
one becomes suspected of evil, and disrepute grows for one.
Even though he does not commit evil deeds himself, he associates with one who does;
he becomes suspicious of evil, and his ill-repute increases.
While serving those who serve, touched by those who touch others,

as an arrow smeared with poison taints the quiver even when it is not itself smeared, so does one become tainted; therefore, out of fear of such tainting, the wise person should never have evil friends.
For by associating with the wicked, one who is touched becomes a toucher of others; as an arrow smeared with poison taints the unsmearable feathers in the quiver,
so a wise person, fearing such tainting, should never become a friend of the wicked.
Just as one knows the ripeness of a fruit within its husk, so should the wise person know his own state; he should not associate with the wicked, but should associate with the virtuous.
Therefore, having seen the ripening of one's own fruit within the very pod,
the wise person should not serve the wicked, but should serve the virtuous.
Even if a fool attends upon the wise for as long as he lives,
he does not understand the Dhamma, just as a spoon does not know the taste of the soup and condiments.
Even if a fool attends upon the wise for as long as he lives,
he does not understand the Dhamma, just as a ladle [does not taste] the flavor of the soup.
Even if one who is wise attends upon a learned person for only a moment,
he quickly understands the Dhamma, just as the tongue perceives the flavors of soup.
Even for a moment, one who is wise attends upon the learned;
he truly understands the Dharma, just as the tongue perceives the flavors of well-prepared soups.
One should not think, "Evil is small; it will not come to me.
Even a water jar is filled by the falling of drops of water.
The fool is filled with evil by accumulating it little by little;
one should not think that evil is small, nor that it will not come upon oneself. Even a large jar is filled by the falling of drops of water.
For fools indeed become full of evils, even by those committed little by little.
One should not think, "The evil is small; it will not come to me."
By the falling of drops of water, even a water-jar is filled;
so too, wisdom is filled by one who gathers merit little by little.
One should not think, "The evil is small; it will not come to me."
By the falling of drops of water, even a large jar is filled;
likewise, fools are filled with evils, even by those committed little by little.
The Chapter on the Fool:
O Daṇḍa,
neither nakedness, nor matted hair, nor mud, nor fasting, nor sleeping on the bare ground [purify one].
They cleanse themselves with dust and rags, crouching on their heels, yet they have not crossed over their doubt regarding death.
Neither wandering naked, nor matted hair, nor smearing with mud, nor fasting, nor sleeping on the bare ground,
nor dust and dirt, nor the practice of sitting in a crouching posture can purify a mortal who has not crossed over his doubts.

Even if adorned, one who lives in equanimity— tamed, peaceful, self-controlled, and walking in the Dharma, having laid aside the rod toward all living beings— he is a brahmin, he is a śramaṇa, he is a bhikṣu.
Even if adorned, one should lead a holy life—patient, self-controlled, disciplined, and practicing celibacy;
having laid aside the rod toward all living beings, he is a Brāhmaṇa, he is a Śramaṇa, he is a Bhikṣu.
Do not speak harshly to anyone; for if addressed thus, they may retort.
For contentious speech is painful, and retaliatory blows may strike you.
Do not speak harshly to anyone; for when addressed, people respond in kind. Indeed, words of agitation lead to suffering, as they surely touch upon retaliatory punishment.
If you agitate yourself like a struck gong,
you will long experience the cycle of birth and death.
If you always drive yourself like a broken pot,
you will indeed experience the cycle of birth and death for a long time.
If you do not disturb yourself, like a bronze vessel that has not been struck, you have attained Nibbāna; for you no longer possess any impulse of aggression.
But you do not stir yourself up, like a gong that has not been struck;
you have reached Nirvana, for no agitation exists within you.
Just as a cowherd drives his cattle to pasture with a staff,
so do old age and death drive living beings onward.
Just as a cowherd drives his cattle to the pasture with a staff,
so do diseases drive the life-span of men toward old age and death.
Just as a cowherd protects the cows of his masters with a staff, so should you protect yourselves; let not the opportune moment pass you by.
For those who have let the moment pass grieve when they are cast into hell.
"Just as a cowherd protects the cows of his masters with a staff, so should you protect yourselves; let not the opportune moment pass you by.
For those who have missed the moment, being cast into the hells, lament."
All tremble at the rod; to all, life is dear.
Making oneself the analogy, one should neither kill nor cause another to kill.
All fear punishment; life is dear to all.
Making oneself the standard of comparison, one should neither kill nor cause others to kill.
He who, seeking his own happiness, harms with violence those beings who desire happiness, does not obtain happiness after death.
He who, seeking his own happiness, harms with violence living beings who desire happiness, will indeed not obtain happiness.
He who, seeking his own happiness, does not harm with violence those beings who desire happiness, obtains happiness after death.
He who, seeking his own happiness, does not harm with violence living beings who also desire happiness, attains happiness after death.
One should not associate with evil friends; one should not associate with base persons. A wise person should associate with the learned; one should associate with the best of men.
For one who associates with such as these, there is progress and not decline.
One should not associate with an evil friend, nor should one associate with the lowest of men;
one should associate with a virtuous friend and associate with the most excellent of persons. For one who associates with such as these, there is welfare and not evil.
Like one who reveals a hidden treasure, he whom one sees as a destroyer of faults—
a wise man who speaks with restraint— one should associate with such a person.
For one who associates with such a person, there is progress, not decline.
One should always attend upon such a wise person who restrains others from wrongdoing, who teaches the truth, who perceives what is blameworthy, and who speaks with firm resolve;
for one who attends upon such a person, there is spiritual welfare and not evil.
One should advise, one should instruct, and one should restrain from what is unwholesome;
for this is pleasing to the virtuous, but it is displeasing to the wicked.
One should instruct and admonish them, and restrain them from what is improper;
thus one does not become dear to the wicked, but becomes dear to the virtuous.
For them, there is a different destiny for the virtuous and the non-virtuous:
the non-virtuous go to hell, while the virtuous are destined for heaven.
Both the wicked and the virtuous go to different states after passing away from here:
the wicked go to hell, while the virtuous are destined for heaven.
This man who has heard little grows old like an ox;
his flesh increases, but his wisdom does not increase.
A heedless man who consorts with another's wife encounters four states:
the acquisition of demerit, an undesired death, reproach as the third, and hell as the fourth.
A man who is heedless and who consorts with another's wife falls into four states:
the loss of merit, sleeping in discomfort, reproach as the third, and hell as the fourth.
There is the acquisition of demerit and an evil rebirth; the pleasure of one who is afraid with one who is afraid is meager;
even the king inflicts heavy punishment, and upon the dissolution of the body, he goes to hell.
One gains no merit and an evil destination; for one who is afraid, there is only meager pleasure with those who are afraid.
Furthermore, the king inflicts heavy punishment, and after the dissolution of the body, one is cooked in the hells.
Those who are self-restrained go to a happy destination; those who are unrestrained go to a miserable destination.
Do not place your trust [in others]; thus, O Vindu, practice with equanimity.
Do not approach the elephant, O elephant; there is suffering for one who eats the flesh of an elephant.
For there is no happy rebirth, O elephant, for one slain by an elephant after this life.
Do not harm this hero among men, who wanders through mountain fastnesses, whose domain is the mountain ridges, who is free from fear, and whose stride is extraordinary.
Like an elephant in battle when arrows are shot from the bow, I endure excessive abuse; for the majority of people are indeed ill-behaved.
Like a nāga in battle, I endure the arrows flying from the bow—
exceedingly harsh words— for the great multitude is indeed ill-behaved.
In times of great fear, many seek refuge in sticks, in mountains, and in forests.
People, terrified by fear, take refuge in various objects and trees.
Driven by fear, many people go for refuge to mountains and forests, to groves and sacred trees.
This refuge is not secure; this refuge is not supreme.
By coming to this refuge, one is released from all suffering.
For this is not a secure refuge; this is not the supreme refuge.
Having come to this refuge, one is not liberated from all suffering.
But he who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha,
and perceives the four noble truths as they truly are—
But when one who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha perceives the Four Noble Truths with wisdom, [he is a true disciple].
This indeed is the secure refuge; this is the supreme refuge.
By coming to this refuge, one is liberated from all suffering.
For this indeed is the secure refuge; this is the supreme refuge. Having come to this refuge, one is liberated from all suffering.
If, when cows are crossing, the leader goes crookedly,
they all go crookedly because the leader has gone crookedly.
In the same way, among human beings, if even he who is esteemed as the best practices unrighteousness, how much more so will the rest of the people?
When the bull leader goes straight as the cows are crossing,
they all go straight when the leader has gone straight.
In the same way, among human beings, if he who is esteemed as the best practices the Dharma, how much more so will other people do the same?
One should practice the Dhamma with good conduct; one should not practice misconduct.
One who lives according to the Dhamma sleeps happily in this world and in the next.
One should practice the Dharma well and not practice misconduct;
for one who practices the Dharma sleeps happily both in this world and in the next.
One should practice the Dhamma with good conduct and not practice misconduct;
the one who lives the holy life (brahmacārī) rests happily in this world and in the world beyond.
Delighting in the Dhamma, rejoicing in the Dhamma, reflecting upon the Dhamma,
and recollecting the Dhamma, a bhikkhu does not fall away from the Dhamma.
Delighting in the Dharma, rejoicing in the Dharma, reflecting only upon the Dharma,
and recollecting the Dharma, a bhikṣu does not fall away from the Dharmas.
Indeed, Dharma protects the one who lives according to Dharma; Dharma, when well-practiced, leads to happiness.
This is the benefit of Dharma well-practiced: the one who lives according to Dharma does not go to an evil destination.
Dharma always protects the practitioner of Dharma; Dharma, when well-practiced, bestows happiness.
This is the benefit of Dharma well-practiced: the practitioner of Dharma does not go to an evil rebirth.
Indeed, the Dhamma protects the one who lives according to the Dhamma; the Dhamma well-practiced leads to happiness.
This is the benefit of the Dhamma well-practiced: the practitioner of the holy life does not go to an evil destination.
Having failed to practice the holy life and having failed to acquire wealth in their youth,
they brood like aged herons in a pond where the fish have vanished.
Having failed to practice the holy life and having failed to acquire wealth in their youth,
they brood like aged cranes in a small pond with few fish.
Having failed to practice the holy life and having acquired no wealth in their youth, they lie like discarded bows, sighing over the past.
Having failed to practice the holy life and having failed to acquire wealth in their youth, they lie down like scattered bows, brooding over the past.
The mindful exert themselves; they do not delight in a dwelling.
Like swans leaving a pond, they abandon home after home.
Possessing mindfulness, they apply themselves to practice; they do not delight in a dwelling.
Like swans leaving a pond, they abandon their home and the flood.
Like swans traveling through the path of the sun through the air by means of psychic power,
the wise emerge from the world, having crushed Māra’s army.
On the path of the sun, like swans, those endowed with the faculty of life travel through the sky;
having crushed Māra’s army, those wise ones depart from the worlds.
What hope, what joy can there be while [the world] is constantly ablaze?
Cast into darkness, do you not seek a lamp?
What joy, what delight can there be when things are thus ablaze? You have entered into darkness; why do you not seek a lamp?
Or like a frontier city well-guarded within and without—thus protect yourselves; let not the opportune moment pass you by. For those who have let the moment pass grieve when they are cast into hell.

Just as a frontier city is guarded, secure both within and without, so should you guard yourselves; let not the opportune moment pass you by. For those who have missed the moment, having been cast into the hells, lament in grief.
One is not a śramaṇa by virtue of being shaven-headed if one lacks the vows and speaks falsehood;
how can one who is possessed by desire and greed be a śramaṇa?
One is not a śramaṇa merely by virtue of being shaven-headed, for one who speaks untruth while unrestrained—
how can such a person, possessed by desire and greed, be a śramaṇa?
But he who completely pacifies evils, both small and great— he alone among those called "śramaṇas" is truly called a "śramaṇa" because of his pacification of evils.
By whomsoever evil has been stilled in every way, whether subtle or gross;
because of the stilling of evils, indeed, one is called a *śramaṇa*.
In whom thirty-six violent streams consisting of the contact of conceit flow,
carrying away wrong view through intentions that are fierce and sharp.
For he whose thirty-six channels, which are the outflows of the mind,
constantly carry the currents of false views through volitions based on greed.
One should abandon anger and utterly cast off pride; one should transcend all fetters.
For one who is unattached to name-and-form and possesses nothing, sufferings do not pursue them.
One should abandon anger and utterly cast off pride; one should transcend all fetters.
For him who is unattached to name and form, being possessed of nothing, no attachments arise.
The Chapter on Refuges:
Patience is the supreme austerity; the Buddhas declare that nibbāna is the supreme.
For one who harms others is not a renunciant; one who torments others is not a śramaṇa.
Patience is the supreme austerity; endurance is what the Buddhas call the highest Nirvana. For one who harms others is not a renunciant, nor does one who oppresses others truly become a śramaṇa.
Those sages who are non-violent and always restrained in body go to the deathless state, where having gone, one does not grieve.
The sages are indeed non-violent, always restrained in body;
they go to the imperishable abode where one who has gone does not grieve.
The disciples of Gotama are always fully awakened,
they whose minds, by day and by night, delight in non-violence.
These disciples of Gautama awaken with a perfect awakening,
they whose minds, both by day and by night, delight in non-violence.
The disciples of Gotama are always well-awakened,
they whose minds delight in meditative cultivation by day and by night.
These disciples of Gautama awaken with a perfect awakening,
they whose minds delight in Nirvana both by day and by night.
The disciples of Gotama are always well-awakened,
for day and night they constantly maintain mindfulness directed toward the body.
These disciples of Gautama awaken with a perfect awakening,
they whose mindfulness directed toward the body is constant, both by day and by night.
Even the gods envy those wise ones who have given birth to meditative absorption, who delight in renunciation and tranquility— the mindful and perfectly awakened ones.
The gods always envy those wise ones who are devoted to meditation, who delight in renunciation and tranquility, and who possess the glory of the Buddhas.
Whether in the forest or in the village, whether in the lowlands or on the high ground—
wherever the Arhats dwell, that place is delightful.
Whether in a village or in a forest, whether on low ground or on high ground—
wherever the Arhats dwell, those regions are delightful.
If one with a virtuous mind and free from malice extends loving-kindness even toward a single living being, one becomes wholesome thereby;
and if one feels compassion for all living beings with the mind, that noble one produces abundant merit.
If one with an uncorrupted mind extends loving-kindness even toward a single living being, by that he would indeed gain merit;
but the noble one, feeling compassion for all beings with his mind, produces abundant merit.
Those royal seers who, having conquered the earth with its seven continents, wandered about performing sacrifices—
the horse sacrifice, the human sacrifice, the *sammāpāsa*, the *vāyupeya*, and the *niraggala*—
do not equal even a sixteenth part of one whose mind of loving-kindness has been well-cultivated.
All [of them] are like the host of stars compared to the moonlight.
But he who, with a mind of loving-kindness, has compassion for all living beings— his loving-kindness extends toward all creatures, and he bears no enmity toward anyone.
He who, with a mind free from malice, has compassion for all beings, is friendly toward all sentient beings; he harbors no enmity toward anyone.
He whose mind delights in non-violence throughout all days and nights,
who has loving-kindness for all beings— by him no enmity is harbored against anyone.
He whose mind delights in non-violence throughout all days and nights, who has loving-kindness toward all beings— for him there is no enmity with anyone.
For one who constantly maintains mindfulness directed toward the body throughout all days and nights,
and who holds loving-kindness toward all beings, there is enmity with nothing whatsoever.
He who neither kills nor causes to kill, neither conquers nor causes to conquer, has loving-kindness for all beings; he has no enmity toward anyone.
For in this world, enmities are never stilled by enmity; rather, they are stilled by non-enmity. This is the eternal law.
For enmities are never appeased in this world by enmity;
enmities are appeased by forbearance—this is the eternal law.
But others do not realize that we have conquered this enmity here;
yet those who do realize it there, the wise, become peaceful because of that.
For others do not understand that "we are striving here";
but for those who do understand this, their quarrels are stilled.
"Truly we live in great happiness, being without enmity among those who harbor enmity;
we dwell without enmity among men who harbor enmity."
"Truly we live in great happiness, being without enmity among those who harbor enmity;
indeed, we dwell without enmity among men who are full of enmity."
"Truly we live in great happiness, free from longing among those who long;
we dwell without longing among men who are full of longing."
Truly we live in great happiness, for while others are anxious, we are free from anxiety;
among anxious men, we indeed dwell without anxiety.
"Truly we live in great happiness, we who possess nothing;
among people who possess things, we dwell as those who possess nothing."
"O, how happily we live, for us there is nothing that belongs to us!
While Mithilā is burning, nothing of ours is burned."
As one would look upon a bubble, as one would look upon a mirage—
so regarding the world, the King of Death does not see him who observes it thus.
Just as one might look upon a bubble, just as one might look upon a mirage—
so indeed beholding the world, one does not see the King of Death.
