This body is worn out, a nest of disease, and fragile; this putrid mass will break apart, for life indeed ends in death.
This form is utterly decayed, a nest of disease, and fragile;
it will undoubtedly break apart as putrid matter, for life indeed ends in death.

Having seen one who was dejected and suffering, and having seen a diseased person and a hungry ghost, before long, a sharp and vast sense of spiritual urgency arose in the youth; the steadfast one severed the bonds of household life.

Having seen here one who was decrepit, and likewise one who was diseased, and having seen one who was dead with his senses departed, that steadfast man abandoned the bonds of home; for the desires of the world are not easily cast off.
Chapter on Patience:
Few among human beings are those people who reach the further shore; they are as rare as those free from taints.
Then these other creatures merely run along the shore.
Few among humans are those people who go to the further shore; but these other beings merely run along the near bank.
But those people who follow the Dharma in the Dharma well-expounded,
they shall go beyond the realm of death, so difficult to cross.
But those people who, when the Dharma has been correctly proclaimed, perceive the Dharma accordingly, will go entirely to the further shore of the domain of death.
Having abandoned which qualities, O wise ones, should you cultivate the bright states,
having come from home to homelessness, where solitude is far removed?
Abandoning dark qualities, cultivate the bright ones, O monks;
having gone from home to homelessness, you should increase your seclusion.
Seeking delight therein, having abandoned sensual pleasures and possessing nothing,
you should thoroughly restrain yourself and the mind from all defilements.
Therein the Noble One finds delight, having abandoned sensual desires and being without possessions;
he should thoroughly restrain himself, his mind from all defilements.
He whose mind is well-cultivated and balanced through the factors of enlightenment—
Those who delight in the relinquishing of the self without grasping,
whose taints are exhausted and who possess radiance— they have attained final liberation in this world.
Those whose minds have been rightly cultivated in the factors of enlightenment,
who have relinquished grasping and rely upon non-grasping— having exhausted their taints and vomited out their faults, they are extinguished in this world.
What ought to be done is neglected, while what ought not to be done is performed;
for those who are arrogant and heedless, their taints increase.
That which ought to be done is neglected, while that which ought not to be done is performed again;
for those who are arrogant and heedless, their taints increase.
And for those whose mindfulness directed toward the body is always well-undertaken,
who do not engage in what should not be done and who act with persistence in what should be done—
for those who are mindful and clearly comprehending, the taints are exhausted.
And for those who have constantly and well applied mindfulness directed toward the body,
they do not engage in what should not be done; being constant in doing what should be done,
mindful and clearly comprehending, their taints are exhausted.
For those who constantly look at the faults of others and are always full of reproach, their taints increase; they are far from the destruction of the taints.
For those who look for the faults of others and constantly harbor thoughts of malice, their taints increase; they remain far from the destruction of the taints.
For those who are devoted to wakefulness, who train themselves day and night,
and who are intent upon Nibbāna, the taints come to an end.
For those devoted to wakefulness, training themselves day and night,
and who are intent upon the deathless, the taints come to an end.

Those whose taints are utterly exhausted and who are no longer dependent on nutriment, for whom emptiness, the signless, and liberation are their sphere of activity— their track is as difficult to follow as that of birds in the sky.
For those whose existence is utterly exhausted and who do not rely on the future limit,
for whom emptiness, the signless, and meditative concentration are the very sphere of activity—
their track is as difficult to follow as that of birds in the sky.
For it is not by mere moral conduct and vows, nor again by great learning, nor by the attainment of meditative concentration, nor by dwelling in solitude.
Neither by mere moral conduct and vows, nor again by great learning,
nor likewise by the attainment of meditative concentration, nor by dwelling in seclusion.
We have touched the bliss of renunciation, which is not practiced by ordinary people;
the monks have attained confidence even though they have not yet reached the destruction of the taints.
A monk should place his trust [in this], for even before the destruction of the outflows is attained,
he shall touch the bliss of perfect awakening, which is not frequented by base men.
This is not the time to be negligent before reaching the destruction of one's own impurities; suffering brings the heedless, just as a lioness brings a deer.
This is not the time for negligence, for while one's own defilements have not yet been exhausted,
Māra follows after the heedless one, just as a lioness follows a deer.
Some enter the womb; those of evil deeds go to hell;
those of good conduct go to heaven; and those free from taints attain final Nirvana.
Just as a lake is deep, serene, and undisturbed,
so do the wise become serene when they have mastered the teachings.
Just as a lake that is very deep, serene, and indeed untroubled,
so too do the wise become serene upon hearing the true Dharma.
Whose victory is never defeated, whose victory the Ender does not approach—
that Buddha of peerless stride, trackless one— whither will you lead him by what path?
Whose victory is never overcome, who follows no one else’s victory in this world—
by what path will you lead that Buddha, whose range is infinite and who is trackless?
By what path will you lead that Buddha, whose trackless state has no footprints, who possesses no craving—the ensnaring and clinging thing—that might lead him anywhere? His range is infinite.
For one who has no entangling, clinging craving that leads through the world— by what path will you lead that Buddha of infinite range, who is trackless?
The Chapter on the Outflows:
He who guards his speech with speech, is well-restrained in mind, and does not practice unwholesome deeds with the body;
Having purified these three paths of action, he shall attain the unsurpassed state of peace.
Guarding one's speech, well-restrained in mind, and likewise performing no unwholesome deed with the body—
one who purifies these auspicious paths of action shall attain the path proclaimed by the Seers.
One should guard against bodily corruption and be restrained in body;
having abandoned bodily misconduct, one should practice good conduct with the body.
One should guard against bodily malice and be well-restrained in body;
having abandoned bodily misconduct, one should practice good conduct with the body.
One should guard against verbal corruption and be restrained in speech;
having abandoned the utterance of evil words, one should practice good conduct of speech.
One should guard against the corruption of speech and remain restrained in words;
having abandoned misconduct of speech, one should practice good conduct of speech.
One should guard against mental corruption and be restrained in mind;
having abandoned mental misconduct, one should practice good conduct with the mind.
One should guard against mental corruption and remain restrained in mind;
having abandoned mental misconduct, one should practice mental good conduct.
The wise are restrained in body, in speech, and in mind;
the wise are restrained in every way—they are indeed well-restrained.
The wise are restrained in body; the wise are well-restrained in speech;
the wise are restrained in mind; the wise are restrained in every way.
This is ancient, O Ādhora; it is not only of the present:
they blame one who sits in silence, they blame one who speaks sparingly, and they also blame one who speaks much; there is no one in the world who is not blamed.
This is ancient, O Ādhora, not something that has only just arisen:
they blame one who sits in silence, they blame one who speaks much, and they blame one who speaks little; there is no one in the worlds who is beyond blame.
There has never been, there will never be, nor is there found at present,
any person who is either entirely blameworthy or entirely praiseworthy.
A person who is either entirely censured or entirely praised.
There has never been, there will not be, nor is there now,
anything that fools— who are established in what is not Dhamma— might honor or revile;
for that which is done by the ignorant and the unintelligent is of no benefit to anyone.
And that which the wise praise after investigating it day by day:
the flawless conduct of the intelligent one, who is composed through wisdom and virtue.
But those who are wise, having investigated what is auspicious and what is inauspicious, praise one who is intelligent,
endowed with good conduct, wise, and restrained in his moral virtues.
Who is worthy to censure him who is like a coin of Jāmbūnada gold?
Even the gods praise him; he is praised even by Brahmā.
A man does not become a person of good character merely by his speech or by his physical appearance; he may be lustful, envious, and deceitful.
A man does not become truly virtuous merely by his name or by the abundance of his physical beauty; he may be a deceiver, envious, and dishonest.
In whom there is truth, the Dhamma, abstinence, self-restraint, and self-control— he, having vomited out his faults, is wise and is called one of virtuous form.
He who possesses faith, virtuous conduct, non-violence, self-restraint, and self-control— he,
having cast off all faults and being wise, is called one who has the form of a sage.
Even if he speaks much that is meaningful, the heedless man who does not act accordingly is no partaker of the ascetic life,
just as a cowherd counting the cattle of others is not a sharer in their value.
Even if he speaks much here that is consistent with the truth, a man who is heedless does not act accordingly;
like a cowherd counting the cows of others, he does not partake in the fruit of the ascetic life.
Even if one speaks but little that is meaningful, if one lives in accordance with the Dharma,
having abandoned passion, hatred, and delusion, with mind liberated, free from harshness and doubt,
and not grasping at anything here or hereafter, such a person partakes in the fruit of asceticism.
Even if one speaks only a little, if it is spoken in harmony and one acts in accordance with the Dharma,

and having abandoned passion, hatred, and likewise delusion— with mind liberated, free from harshness and doubt, and not grasping at this world or the next— one becomes a partaker of the fruit of asceticism.
One should speak the truth, one should not be angry, and one should give even a little when asked;
by these three qualities, one goes into the presence of the gods.
One should speak the truth, one should not become angry, and one should give even from what is little;
endowed with these three states, one shall go into the presence of the gods.
Indeed, the miserly do not go to the world of the gods, for fools do not praise giving;
but the wise person, rejoicing in the gift, goes to the world of the gods by that very act.
Indeed, misers do not go to the world of the gods, for they are fools who do not praise giving;
but one who is faithful and even rejoices in the gift will likewise become happy in the future life.
People hold dear one who is virtuous, pure, capable, established in the Dhamma, truthful, self-reliant, and peaceful.
People hold dear that person who abides in the Dharma, who is endowed with virtue, possessed of a sense of shame, truthful in speech, self-reliant, and peaceful.
Better it would be to eat glowing iron balls, resembling tongues of fire,
than that one of immoral conduct and unrestrained should consume the alms-food of the nation.
For it would be better to eat glowing iron balls, heated like flames of fire,
than for one of immoral conduct and unrestrained self to consume the alms of a kingdom.
Just as a blade of kusa grass, if wrongly grasped, cuts the very hand, so too the ascetic life, if wrongly practiced, leads one toward hell.
Just as a poorly grasped arrow cuts the very hand that holds it,
so too does the ascetic life, when wrongly practiced, drag one down into the hells.
For a person who has transgressed this one Dhamma— the speaker of falsehood—
who has cast aside the world beyond, there is no evil deed that he will not do.
For even a well-sharpened, deadly poison from the Hālāhala snake is not so feared as ill-spoken speech,
which brings about such swift destruction.
As a person is being born, an axe is born in his mouth,
with which he cuts himself by speaking ill-spoken words.
For a person who is born, an axe is indeed born within his mouth,
with which he cuts himself by speaking ill-spoken words.
For he who praises one who deserves blame, or blames one who deserves praise, sows discord with his mouth; by that discord, he finds no happiness.
He who praises those who deserve blame and blames those who deserve praise gathers that strife with his own mouth; by means of that strife, he finds no happiness.
Trifling is this misfortune that one loses wealth at dice;
far greater is the misfortune that one loses everything, even one’s own self.
Whoever harbors malice toward the Sugatas,
this is indeed a trifling quarrel— namely, one who loses his wealth here at dice;
far greater than that is the quarrel of one who harbors malice toward the Sugatas.
One hundred thousand and thirty-six *nirabbudas*, plus five *abbudas*—
this is the duration for which one who reviles the noble ones goes to hell, having directed speech and mind toward evil.
One hundred thousand, thirty-six,
and five *arbuda* hells does the reviler of the noble ones enter, having directed his speech and mind toward evil.
One should speak only what is auspicious; one should not utter what is evil. Release is better for the auspicious one, but once released, the evil one suffers.
One should release a virtuous woman, but never release a wicked one;
for a virtuous woman is better when released, whereas a wicked woman brings remorse when released.
One should serve only the auspicious; one should not be released by the evil.
Release is better for the auspicious; once released, the evil one suffers.
One should speak auspicious words and not utter what is evil; one should restrain anger as it arises, for thus it ceases like poison.
One should speak auspicious words and not utter what is evil;
the wise person should abandon ignorance, for by that [ignorance], one is destroyed.
The Chapter on Speech.
He who has taken up extreme misconduct, like a creeper entwining a sal tree,
makes himself such that he desires his own destruction.
He who is utterly immoral makes himself such that his enemies wish him ill, just like a *sālavān* tree that is destroyed from its very roots.
For the evil committed by oneself, born of oneself, and originating from oneself,
clings to the fool, just as lac adheres to a bamboo reed.
The evil committed by oneself, born of oneself and originating from oneself,
crushes that very person, just as a diamond crushes a stone gem.
By oneself indeed is evil done; by oneself is one defiled.
By oneself is evil left undone; by oneself is one purified. Purity and impurity belong to oneself; no one can purify another.
For when one has committed an evil deed by oneself, one is always tormented by oneself;
but when one has not committed an evil deed by oneself, one is purified by oneself alone. One whose own mind is impure cannot purify another.
One should not look at the faults of others, nor at what has been done or left undone by others;
rather, one should observe for oneself those things that have been done and those that have been left undone.
One should not look at the faults of others, nor at what others have done or left undone; rather, one should examine only oneself—both one's own equanimity and one's own failings.
One should not look for the faults of others, nor for their equals and unequals;
rather, one should examine oneself for what is equal and what is unequal.
If you would know yourself as dear, you should guard yourself well;
for such happiness is not easily obtained by those who do evil deeds.
If one should know oneself to be dear, one should not join it with evil;
for happiness is not easily obtained by one who performs wicked deeds.
If one holds oneself dear, one should guard oneself well;
a wise person should keep watch over at least one of the three watches of the night.
If one knows oneself to be dear, one should protect it well-guarded;
a wise person should remain vigilant during one of these three watches of the night.
Sitting alone, lying down alone, wandering alone, and untiring,
one who delights in being alone will find joy at the edge of the forest.
Unwearied, one should find delight in a single seat, a single bed, and a solitary course; one should always dwell alone in the forests, delighting only in the Self.
The fool who opposes the teaching of the Arhats, the Noble Ones who live by the Dhamma, relying on an evil view,
makes himself such as poison would wish him to be.
The foolish person who reviles the teaching of the Arhats, the Noble Ones who live according to the Dhamma, and relies upon an evil view,
bears fruit for his own destruction like the thorny bamboo.
The one of dull intellect who, relying on an evil view, reviles the teaching of the Arhats— the noble ones who live by the Dharma—
bears fruit for his own destruction, just as the thorny fruit of the kaṇṭaka tree.
First, one should establish oneself in what is meaningful and in the Dhamma;
then one may instruct others, saying, "May they become just as I am."
One should first establish oneself in what is appropriate;
then one may instruct another, just as I am.
First, one should establish oneself in what is appropriate;
then, instructing others, the wise person will not be defiled.
One should first establish oneself in what is appropriate;
thereafter, one may instruct others, for thus the wise person does not suffer.
One should act oneself in the same way that one would instruct another;
for indeed, it is said that the self is difficult to tame, yet one who is untamed should surely tame it.
One should indeed discipline oneself in such a way that one would instruct another;
"Ah, my own self must always be well-tamed, for it is exceedingly difficult to tame."
For one’s own self, when tamed, is better than other offspring;
for the person who has tamed themselves and always lives with restraint.
For one who has conquered the self is better than one who has conquered these other beings— such is the case for the man who is self-restrained and whose conduct is ever-disciplined.
Neither gods nor gandharvas, nor Māra together with Brahmā,
could overturn the victory of such a person;
neither gods, nor gandharvas, nor Māra, even together with Brahmā.
They might cause the defeat of one already defeated; so it is with a wise monk.
For oneself is indeed one's own protector; for who else could be a protector?
Through a self well-conducted, one obtains a protector that is difficult to find.
The self, indeed, is the master of the self; for who else could be the master? For by means of a well-tamed self, the wise person gains a true master.
For oneself is indeed one's own protector; for oneself is indeed one's own refuge.
Therefore, one should restrain oneself, as a merchant restrains a noble horse.
For oneself alone is one's own protector; oneself is the refuge of oneself.
Therefore, restrain yourself as a charioteer restrains a noble steed.
One should always tame oneself with the easy-goingness of a horse; be disciplined, peaceful, and upright, and thereby become free from crookedness.
Then, being tamed, one becomes happy; through non-clinging, one attains cessation.
One should tame oneself alone, as a charioteer tames a noble horse.
Be disciplined, serene, and upright; then become free from crookedness.
Then, being tamed, you will be happy; through non-clinging, you will be extinguished.
Urge yourself by yourself, examine yourself by yourself;
guarded by yourself and mindful, you, O monk, will dwell in happiness.
One should not neglect one's own welfare for the sake of another's welfare, however great it may be;
having recognized that others have their own welfare, one should be devoted solely to one's own welfare.
One should not neglect one's own welfare, even for the sake of another’s welfare, however great it may be;
having recognized that one's own welfare is supreme, one should be intent upon achieving that goal.
Neither for his own sake nor for the sake of another, he should not desire heaven, wealth, or a kingdom;
he should not desire his own prosperity through unrighteousness—he, being virtuous, wise, and righteous, would be such a one.
The Chapter on Oneself:
People give gifts according to their faith and according to their devotion.
In this regard, he who is displeased with the food and drink of others does not attain concentration by day or by night.
Some people give according to their faith and according to their means;
in that regard, he who becomes displeased at the food and drink of others does not attain meditative concentration by day or by night.
But for one by whom this has been utterly cut off at the root,
that person indeed attains concentration both by day and by night.
But he for whom these [defilements] have been utterly severed, cut down like the tops of palm trees,
indeed attains meditative concentration by day and by night.
Like a noble horse touched by the whip, they wander with ardent energy and self-possession;
through faith, virtue, vigor, concentration, and the discernment of the Dharma— established in patience, gentleness, and concentration— they have attained the essence of learning and wisdom.
Just as a noble horse, when touched by the whip, moves with ardent energy and vigilance, so too one who is faithful,
endowed with the virtues of morality, concentrated, and skilled in the discernment of the Dharma—
possessing perfected knowledge and conduct, mindful, and a protector— abandons all suffering.
He who, in this very life, attains faith and unsurpassed wisdom—he indeed possesses great wealth in the world; all other wealth is but trivial.
Whatever wise person in this world of living beings obtains faith and wisdom—that indeed is their supreme wealth; all other wealth is inferior.
Endowed with faith and perfected in virtue, established in fame and wealth,
whatever region he frequents, there he is honored.
One who is faithful, endowed with virtue, generous, and free from envy is honored wherever he may go.
A person who walks with faith as his companion— no one can find him lacking, for even if he were without faith in his conduct,
fame and renown come to him from that, and after casting off the body, he goes to heaven.
The man who lacks faith, who is ungrateful, who severs his ties,
who has destroyed all opportunity, and who eats what has been vomited up— he indeed is the supreme person.
The man who is faithless, ungrateful, and a breaker of alliances— he who has destroyed his own opportunity and vomits up what he has eaten— is indeed the supreme person.
Rare is the arising of Buddhas; rare is the teaching of the Dharma;
rare is the attainment of faith; rare is the life of mortals.
For one whose mind is unsettled, who does not understand the true Dharma,
and whose confidence is wavering, wisdom does not reach fulfillment.
For one whose mind is unstable, who does not understand the true Dharma,
and whose faith is wavering, wisdom is not brought to fulfillment.
The Dharma cannot be understood by one whose mind is not serene, who is corrupt, or who is angry, nor by one who is full of contentiousness.
For the Dharma cannot be understood with a mind that is not serene, or one that is corrupted or agitated, nor by one who is full of impetuosity.
But he who, having subdued agitation and lack of serenity in the mind, possesses a serene heart and is well-disposed— he indeed is worthy of the well-spoken word.
But he who, having subdued agitation and lack of serenity in his mind,
and having cast away all resentment, should understand what is well-spoken;
Compared to the attainment of human birth, the going to the heavenly realms,
and the sovereignty over the entire earth, the fruit of stream-entry is superior.
He whose faith in the Tathāgata is unshakable and well-established,
and whose virtue is beautiful, dear to the noble ones, and praiseworthy—
He who has faith in the Saṅgha and whose vision is upright—
him they call "not poor," and his life is not in vain.
A wise person, remembering the teaching of the Buddhas, should constantly apply themselves to her faith, virtue, and confidence in the vision of the Dharma.
The Chapter on Giving:
The mind is flickering and restless; it is difficult to guard and difficult to restrain.
The wise person makes himself straight, just as an arrow-maker straightens an arrow-shaft.
The mind is flickering, restless, difficult to perceive, and hard to restrain;
the wise man makes it straight, just as an archer does with his skill.
Like a water-born fish cast upon dry land and dragged from its watery home, this mind quivers; let it strive to abandon the realm of Māra.
Like a water-born creature cast onto dry land, or like one pulled from its home out of a torrent, the mind indeed quivers; thus, the realm of Māra must be abandoned.
Those who restrain the mind— which wanders far, moves alone, is bodiless, and dwells in the cave— will be released from the bonds of Māra.
The taming of the mind is excellent—the mind which is difficult to grasp, light, and falling wherever it pleases; a tamed mind brings happiness.
The taming of the mind is excellent—the mind which is difficult to restrain, fickle, and falling wherever it desires; a tamed mind brings happiness.
The wise person should guard the mind, which is so difficult to see, so subtle, and which falls according to its own desires; for when guarded, it brings happiness.
For one who relies on nothing and whose mind is unassailed,
there is no fear for the watchful one who has left behind both good and evil.
For one who relies on nothing and whose mind is unassailed,
there is no fear for the watchful one who has left behind both good and evil.
Drinking the flavor of delight in the Dharma with a serene mind,
the wise person always rejoices in the Dharma proclaimed by the Noble Ones.
One who delights in the Dharma sleeps happily with a serene mind;
the wise and mindful person finds joy in the Dharma proclaimed by the Noble Ones.
Soon indeed this body will lie upon the earth, cast away, devoid of consciousness, like a useless log of wood.
Alas, before long this body will lie upon the earth,
empty and devoid of consciousness, like a discarded log of wood.

Having understood this body to be like a jar and having established the mind as being like a city, one should fight Māra with the weapon of wisdom; and having conquered him, one should guard the victory, remaining without attachment.

Having understood this body to be like a jar and the mind established as being like a city, one should fight Māra with the weapon of wisdom; and having conquered him, one should guard it, remaining without a dwelling-place.
Just as fire penetrates a poorly thatched house,
so does lust penetrate an untrained mind.
For just as rain thoroughly penetrates a poorly thatched house,
so does passion thoroughly penetrate an uncultivated mind.
Just as rain does not penetrate a well-thatched house,
so passion does not penetrate a well-developed mind.
For just as rain does not penetrate a well-thatched house,
so passion does not penetrate a well-cultivated mind.
Just as rain penetrates a poorly thatched house,
so does lust penetrate an untrained mind.
For just as rain breaks through a poorly thatched house,

Just as rain does not penetrate a well-thatched house,
so defilement does not penetrate a well-cultivated mind.
For just as rain does not penetrate a well-thatched house,
so hatred does not penetrate a well-cultivated mind.
Just as rain penetrates a poorly thatched house,
so does delusion penetrate an uncultivated mind.
For just as rain breaks through a poorly thatched house,
so does delusion break through an untrained mind.
Just as rain does not penetrate a well-roofed house,
so delusion does not penetrate a well-developed mind.
For just as rain does not penetrate a well-thatched house,
so delusion does not penetrate a well-cultivated mind.
To refrain from all evil, to cultivate the wholesome,
and to discipline one’s own mind— this is the teaching of the Buddhas.
To refrain from all evil, to cultivate the wholesome,
and to purify one’s own mind— this is the teaching of the Buddha.
The Chapter on the Mind: The Eightfold Path is the best among paths; the Four Noble Truths are the best among truths.
Dispassion is the best of all things; the Visionary is the best among bipeds.
Among paths, the Eightfold Path is supreme; among truths, the Four Noble Truths are supreme; among phenomena, dispassion is supreme; and among bipeds, the one with vision is supreme.
The path for the removal of the arrow of ignorance has been declared by me to you. You yourselves must exert effort; the Tathāgatas are merely the proclaimers.
Those who practice meditation and enter the path shall be liberated from the bonds of Māra.

I have declared to you the path that cuts through the thorn of ignorance; it is by you yourselves that it must be practiced. The Tathāgatas are merely the proclaimers; those who practice it with meditative concentration will abandon the bonds of Māra.
This alone is the path; there is no other for the purification of vision.
Enter upon that path which is the deluder of Māra. By practicing according to these [teachings], you will make an end of suffering.
For this is the path, and there is no other, for the purification of vision:
"Enter upon that path; it is the deluder of Māra.
By practicing according to these [teachings], you shall make an end of suffering."
Cut down the forest, not the trees; from the forest fear is born.
Having cut down both the forest and the undergrowth, you shall go to the state beyond the forest.
"Cut down the forest, not the mere trees; for from the forest indeed arises fear.
Having cut down the forest together with its roots, become free from the forest, O monks."
As long as even an atom’s worth of a forest of craving is not severed among a man’s kinsmen,
his mind remains bound there, like a suckling calf to its mother.
For as long as even a hair’s breadth of forest remains among one's kinsmen, a man’s mind is bound to them; he is like a calf still nursing at its mother.
Having severed his own affection like an autumnal water-lily with one's hand,
and having laid out the very path to peace, he attained Nibbāna as taught by the Sugata.
Cut off your own attachment, just as one plucks an autumn lotus from the water;
cultivate only the path of peace, the Nirvana taught by the Sugata.
"I shall do this in the rainy season; I shall do this in the winter months"—thus the fool thinks, not perceiving the obstacle.
"I shall spend the rainy season here, as well as the winter and the summer"—
thus a fool thinks, failing to see the obstacles.
Death carries away that man who is intoxicated by his children and cattle, whose mind is distracted, just as a great flood sweeps away a sleeping village.
Death seizes and carries away that man who is intoxicated by children and cattle, whose mind is deeply attached [to them], just as a great flood sweeps away a sleeping village.
Sons are not a protection, nor is a father, nor even brothers;
for one who is overcome by the End-Maker, there is no refuge among kinsmen.
Sons are not for protection, nor is a father, nor even kinsmen;
for one overcome by the Ender, they do not become a refuge.
While their kinsmen are thus weeping and lamenting on one side, people pass away; they leave him against their will.
Having understood this, the wise person, possessed of insight and free from stinginess,
should constantly purify that path leading to heaven;
for seeing this, the learned one should always train in the precepts.
One should swiftly purify the path leading to nirvāṇa.
For a wise person, clearly perceiving their own welfare,
should constantly purify that path leading to heaven.
One who is endowed with faith, perfected in virtue, wise, and well-concentrated,
constantly purifies the path that leads to the truth in the life to come.
Endowed with faith and virtuous conduct, wise and well-concentrated,
he delights in cultivating the path, rejoicing in internal tranquility.
Endowed with faith and virtue, always delighting in wisdom,
he goes forth like a fire burning away fetters— both subtle and gross—
as well as pride and evil malice.
Endowed with faith and virtue, always delighting in wisdom,
he goes forth like a fire burning away fetters, both subtle and gross,
as well as pride and evil.
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; when one perceives this through wisdom, one becomes weary of suffering. This is the path to purification.
Always perceiving with wisdom that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, one then becomes weary of suffering; this is the path to purification.
When one perceives with wisdom that "all phenomena are non-self," then one becomes weary of suffering; this is the path to purification.
When one perceives with wisdom that all phenomena are without self, one then becomes weary of suffering; this is the path to purification.
For through application, much arises; through non-application, much is destroyed.
Having understood this path of victory regarding both existence and non-existence, the wise person should train themselves in such a way that their abundance increases.
From union arises existence; from separation comes the cessation of existence.
Having understood this twofold path—leading both to existence and to non-existence—the wise person should train therein so as to transcend all unions.
The Chapter on the Path:
Even if one were to speak a thousand times a thousand words consisting of meaningless phrases, [it would not equal the value of a single meaningful word].
A single meaningful word is better, hearing which one attains tranquility.
Better than a hundred verses composed of meaningless words is a single verse of Dharma, hearing which one attains peace.
A single word of the Dharma is better than a hundred verses composed of meaningless words, for by hearing that one word, one attains peace.
One who conquers a thousand times a thousand men in human battle, yet conquers but one— the self— by means of wisdom, he indeed is the supreme victor in battle.
He who might conquer a thousand times a thousand enemies in battle,
yet he who conquers himself alone— that indeed is the battle difficult to win.
If one were to sacrifice a thousand [offerings] every month for a hundred years,
and another were to honor for even a single moment one whose self is cultivated,
that latter act of honoring is better than the sacrifices performed for a hundred years.
If one were to sacrifice with a thousand [offerings] every month for a hundred years,
yet another were to worship for even a single moment a person whose self is purified,
that act of worship is superior; it is not equal to those hundred years of sacrifice.
If someone were to tend a fire in the forest for a hundred years, and another were to honor for even a moment a person who has cultivated the self—
that act of honoring is far better than those hundred years of sacrifice.
Whether one should tend the sacrificial fire in the forest for a full hundred years,
or whether one should honor for even a single moment a person whose self is cultivated— the latter act of honoring is superior; that hundred-year sacrifice is not equal to it.

Whatever sacrifice or offering one seeking merit performs in the world for a year, all that does not equal even a fourth part of the merit of paying homage to those who are upright; homage to the upright is superior.
One who might sacrifice with a thousand [offerings] every month for a hundred years does not equal even a sixteenth part of the serene confidence placed in the Buddha.
Even if one were to sacrifice with a thousand [offerings] every month for a hundred years,
that would not be worth a sixteenth part of the serene confidence placed in the Buddha.
One who might sacrifice with a thousand [pieces of gold] every month for a hundred years does not equal even a sixteenth part of the serene confidence one has in the Dhamma.
Even if one were to perform sacrifices with a thousand [pieces of gold] every month for a hundred years,
that would not be worth a sixteenth part of the merit of serene faith in the Dharma.
One who might sacrifice a thousand [coins] every month for a hundred years does not equal even a sixteenth part of the confidence placed in the Saṅgha.
Even if one were to sacrifice a thousand [coins] every month for a hundred years,
that would not be worth a sixteenth part of the faith placed in the Saṅgha.
One who might sacrifice with a thousand [pieces of gold] every month for a hundred years does not equal even a sixteenth part of those who have realized the Dhamma.
Even if one were to sacrifice a thousand times every month for a hundred years,
that would not be worth a sixteenth part of the serene confidence placed in the Buddha.
Month after month, a fool might consume food with the tip of a blade of kusha grass;
yet that does not equal even a sixteenth part of the serene confidence placed in the Buddha.
Even if one were to eat food with the tip of a blade of kusha grass month after month,
that would not be worth even a sixteenth part of the serene confidence placed in the Buddha.
Month after month, a fool might eat his food with the tip of a blade of kusha grass;
yet that does not equal even a sixteenth part of the confidence one has in the Dhamma.
Even if one were to eat food with the tip of a blade of kusha grass month after month,

Month after month, a fool might consume his food with the tip of a blade of kusha grass;
yet that does not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of faith in the Sangha.
Even if one were to eat food with the tip of a blade of kusha grass month after month,
that would not be worth even a sixteenth part of the faith placed in the Sangha.
Month after month, a fool might eat his food with the tip of a blade of kusha grass;
yet that does not equal even a sixteenth part of those who have realized the Dharma for themselves.
If one were to eat food with the tip of a blade of kusha grass month after month,

Better than living for a hundred years immoral and unconcentrated is a single day’s life of one who is virtuous and meditative.
Better than living for a hundred years with immoral conduct and an uncollected mind is a single day lived by one who is virtuous and pure.
Better than living for a hundred years, immoral and unconcentrated, is a single day’s life of one who is wise and meditative.
Better than living for a hundred years with poor wisdom and lacking concentration is a single day lived by a wise person who is constantly absorbed in meditation.
Better than living for a hundred years lazy and lacking in vigor is a single day of life for one who exerts firm energy.
Better than living for a hundred years as one who is indolent and lacking in vigor is a single day lived by one who exerts firm energy.
Better than living for a hundred years without seeing the arising and passing away [of phenomena] is a single day's life for one who sees the arising and passing away.
Better than living for a hundred years without perceiving the rise and fall [of all things] is a single day of life for one who perceives that rise and fall.
Better than living for a hundred years without seeing the supreme Dharma is to live for a single day seeing the supreme Dharma.
Though one might live for a hundred years without beholding the deathless state,
a single day’s life of one who beholds the deathless state is better.
Better than living for a hundred years without beholding the immortal state is a single day's life of one who beholds the immortal state.
Though one might live for a hundred years without being established in the true Dharma,
a single day's life here of one who understands the true Dharma is better.
Better than living for a hundred years without attaining the destruction of the taints is a single day of life in which the destruction of the taints is attained.

The Uraga of the thousand-fold assembly,
who has not found any essence in existences, just as one seeking flowers finds none among the udumbara trees.
That bhikkhu abandons both this shore and the far shore, just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin.
He who, having realized that there is no essence in worldly existences— just as one finds no fruit within the flower of the udumbara tree—
that monk abandons this world of the far shore, just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin.
The bhikkhu who subdues arisen lust, like a spreading snake's venom with medicinal herbs,
leaves behind both this shore and the far shore, just as a serpent sheds its worn-out old skin.
The bhikkhu who restrains arisen defilement with medicines, as one would [neutralize] spreading snake venom,
leaves behind both this shore and the further shore, just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin.

The bhikkhu who dispels arisen delusion, as one does the spreading venom of a snake with medicinal herbs— he leaves behind both this shore and the far shore, just as a snake sheds its worn-out old skin.

The bhikkhu who restrains arisen anger, as one would neutralize spreading snake venom with medicines— he leaves behind both this shore and the far shore, just as a serpent sheds its worn-out old skin.

The bhikkhu who restrains arisen conceit, as one would neutralize spreading snake venom with medicinal herbs— he leaves behind both this shore and the far shore, just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin.

The bhikkhu who has uprooted passion without remainder, like one who has plunged into a lake and plucked a lotus flower, leaves behind both this shore and the far shore, just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin.
He who completely cuts off passion, like one diving into the water and plucking a lotus flower,
that monk leaves behind this world beyond, just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin.

The bhikkhu who has eradicated every fault, like one who has plunged into a lake and plucked a lotus flower, leaves behind both this shore and the far shore, just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin.
The monk who utterly cuts off hatred, like one who has plunged into the water and plucked a lotus flower from its root— he leaves this world behind, just as a snake casts off its old, worn-out skin.

The monk who has eradicated delusion without remainder, like one who has plunged into a lake and plucked a lotus flower, leaves behind both this shore and the far shore, just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin.

The monk who cuts off delusion without remainder, like one diving into the water and plucking a lotus flower from its stalk— he indeed leaves this world behind, just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin.

The monk who has eradicated anger without remainder, like one who has plunged into a lake and plucked a lotus flower, leaves behind both this shore and the far shore, just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin.

The monk who has uprooted conceit without remainder, like one who has plunged into a lake and plucked a lotus flower, leaves behind both this shore and the far shore, just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin.

The monk who has eradicated passion without remainder, having severed his bonds like the roots of a *kuśa* plant— he abandons both this shore and the far shore, just as a snake sheds its worn-out, ancient skin.
The bhikkhu who has cut off craving without remainder, having cleared away the swift-flowing river, leaves behind both this shore and the far shore, just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin.
The monk who completely cuts off craving, just as one skilled in draining dries up rivers of swift current— he abandons this shoreless world, just as a snake casts off its old, worn-out skin.
He who does not move forward nor move backward, who has completely transcended this conceptual proliferation—
that bhikkhu leaves behind both this shore and the far shore, just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin.

The monk who neither looks back nor looks forward, [knowing] that all this is false and subject to deception— he leaves behind both this shore and the far shore, just as a snake sheds its worn-out old skin.
He who, knowing this entire world to be false, neither exults nor desponds—
that monk indeed abandons this shoreless state, just as a snake casts off its old, worn-out skin.

That bhikkhu for whom there are no forest-thickets whatsoever— those factors conducive to the cause of bondage and existence— leaves behind both this shore and the far shore, just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin.
For he who has no desires whatsoever and whose root of unwholesomeness is destroyed—
that monk abandons this shoreless world, just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin.
He for whom no thicket of craving exists, whose unwholesome roots have been utterly uprooted—
that bhikkhu abandons both this shore and the far shore, just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin.
He for whom there are no fevers whatsoever, and for whom the root of unwholesomeness has perished—
that monk abandons this shoreless world, just as a snake sheds its old, worn-out skin.
